title: Drug classes I: heart, blood vessels, clotting and metabolism
note: Most drug classes act on one well-defined target: a receptor, an enzyme or a transporter. Name endings often signal the class: -olol (beta blockers), -pril (ACE inhibitors), -sartan (ARBs), -statin (statins), -xaban (factor Xa inhibitors). Knowing the target predicts both the main effect and the classic side effects.

read.title: One hormone system, three drug targets
text: The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system shows how one pathway can be blocked at several points. When blood pressure or kidney blood flow falls, the kidney releases renin. Renin cuts angiotensinogen, a liver protein, into angiotensin I. Angiotensin-converting enzyme, found largely in the lungs, then turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II, which constricts arteries and triggers aldosterone release, so the kidneys retain sodium and water.

ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril block the converting step, lowering angiotensin II. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so blocking it lets bradykinin build up, which is linked to the dry cough and, rarely, the swelling called angioedema. Angiotensin II receptor blockers such as losartan act one step later, blocking the receptor itself; they cause cough much less often because bradykinin is unaffected. Beta blockers act upstream by reducing renin release from the kidney, as well as by slowing the heart.
Because aldosterone normally promotes potassium loss, both ACE inhibitors and ARBs can raise blood potassium, which clinicians monitor.

q.q: Why do ACE inhibitors cause cough more often than ARBs?
Where do ARBs act in the pathway?
Why can ACE inhibitors raise blood potassium?
o: They reduce aldosterone, which normally promotes potassium loss
